extracted.intended_audience: students and instructors of Euclidean solid geometry (advanced secondary / undergraduate)
extracted.subtask_description: A collection of Euclidean solid-geometry definitions, propositions (theorems), corollaries and exercises concerning polyhedra, prisms, pyramids, cylinders, cones and spheres, together with proofs and remarks. Useful as reference material for solving and proving problems in 3D Euclidean geometry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop XX — Trihedral face-angle inequality
rubrics_metrics.description: The sum of any two plane angles (BAD, DAC) of a trihedral angle (A) is greater than the third (BAC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by constructing an equal angle at A and comparing sides of triangles BAD and BAE to show BD = BE, then using triangle-side/angle inequalities to deduce the required inequality. Includes the case-check that if the third angle is ≤ either of the others the proposition is evident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop XXI — Sum of plane angles of a solid angle
rubrics_metrics.description: The sum of all the plane angles (BAC, CAD, …) forming any solid angle (A) is less than four right angles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof reduces to a polygonal cross-section: cut the planes by another plane to form triangles whose base angles sum to more than the interior angles of the polygonal section; compare totals to deduce the plane-angle sum is less than four right angles. Observation: may fail if the polygonal base contains re-entrant angles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation on Prop XXI
rubrics_metrics.description: Caveat: Prop XXI may not hold if the polygonal base BCDEF contains re-entrant (concave) angles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proof assumes convex polygonal cross-sections; re-entrant angles change the inequality relations used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercises on Book XI (summary)
rubrics_metrics.description: A list of exercises related to trihedral and solid angles, incl. inequalities between face angles, construction of planes parallel to non-coplanar lines, common perpendiculars, orthocentre properties, loci, and properties of gauche quadrilaterals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises 1–17 enumerate problems such as: any face angle of a trihedral is less than the sum but greater than the difference of the supplements of the other two (1); draw a common perpendicular to two non-coplanar lines and show it's the shortest distance (4); locus problems and proportionality statements (11–12); constructing right lines intersecting/given non-coplanar lines (15–16). These are given as practice problems with geometric constructions and proofs expected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Def i — Polyhedron and naming by face count
rubrics_metrics.description: A polyhedron is a solid figure bounded by plane figures; named tetrahedron (4 faces), hexahedron (6), octahedron (8), dodecahedron (12), icosahedron (20).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduces vocabulary for solids by number of faces; basis for classification in subsequent propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Def ii — Regular polyhedron
rubrics_metrics.description: If the plane faces of a polyhedron are equal and similar rectilineal figures, the solid is a regular polyhedron.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets the notion of regularity used for later references to Platonic solids and symmetry arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Def iii — Pyramid
rubrics_metrics.description: A pyramid is a polyhedron with all faces but one meeting in a point; the common point is the vertex and the opposite face the base.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard definition used for propositions about pyramids, sections, altitudes and volume.

rubrics_metrics.name: Def iv — Prism
rubrics_metrics.description: A prism is a polyhedron having a pair of parallel faces which are equal and similar rectilineal figures called its ends; the other faces are parallelograms called side faces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition distinguishes ends and side faces; basis for statements about prisms (right/oblique) and volume relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Def v — Right and oblique prism
rubrics_metrics.description: A prism whose ends are perpendicular to its sides is a right prism; any other prism is oblique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in proofs where normals/perpendicularity simplify congruence or volume arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Def vi — Altitude of pyramids and prisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Altitude of a pyramid is the perpendicular from its vertex to its base; altitude of a prism is the perpendicular distance between its ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key for volume formulas and proportional-section corollaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Def vii — Parallelopiped
rubrics_metrics.description: A parallelopiped is a prism whose bases are parallelograms (hence a hexahedron).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in propositions about equality and volume of parallelopipeds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Def viii — Cube
rubrics_metrics.description: A cube is a rectangular parallelopiped all of whose faces are squares.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard special case used later (e.g., volume comparisons with spheres).

rubrics_metrics.name: Def ix — Cylinder (solid of revolution)
rubrics_metrics.description: A cylinder is the solid described by revolving a rectangle about one of its sides (the axis); the circles at the ends are the bases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition used to derive cylinder volume and surface properties via limiting arguments (elementary triangles/prisms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Def x — Cone
rubrics_metrics.description: A cone is the solid described by revolving a right-angled triangle about one of the legs (the axis); the circle described by the other leg is the base.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used for cone volume and surface area relations with cylinder and pyramids.

rubrics_metrics.name: Def xi — Sphere
rubrics_metrics.description: A sphere is the solid described by revolving a semicircle about its diameter (the centre is centre of generating semicircle); any line through the centre terminated by the surface is a diameter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition underpins proofs of sphere volume and surface area via limiting/infinitesimal arguments and relations with circumscribed cylinder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop I — Equality of right prisms with equal similar bases and equal altitudes
rubrics_metrics.description: Right prisms whose bases are equal and similar and whose altitudes are equal are equal solids (congruent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by applying bases to each other; corollaries: (1) right prisms with equal bases and equal altitudes have equal volumes; (2) volumes of right prisms with equal bases are proportional to altitudes; (3) with equal altitudes volumes are proportional to base areas; (4) rectangular parallelopiped volume equals product of three dimensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop II — Equality of parallelopipeds with same base and equal altitudes
rubrics_metrics.description: Parallelopipeds having a common base and equal altitudes are equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof splits into cases depending on edge alignment; corollary: volume of a parallelopiped equals product of base area and altitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop III — Diagonal plane bisects a parallelopiped
rubrics_metrics.description: A diagonal plane of a parallelopiped divides it into two prisms of equal volume.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by decomposing with perpendicular planes; corollaries: triangular prism volume equals product of base area and altitude (half of corresponding parallelopiped), and any prism's volume equals base × altitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop IV — Parallel section of pyramid similar to base
rubrics_metrics.description: If a pyramid is cut by any plane parallel to the base, the section is similar to the base.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses properties of parallel lines and similar triangles; corollaries: edges/altitude are proportionally divided, areas of parallel sections are in duplicate ratio of distances from vertex, and corresponding sections of two pyramids with same altitude ratio are proportional to bases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop V — Equal-base-and-altitude pyramids have equal volumes
rubrics_metrics.description: Pyramids having equal altitudes and bases of equal areas have equal volumes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by contradiction using division into thin prism-slices and comparison; corollaries: triangular pyramid volume is one-third of prism with same base and altitude; every pyramid's volume is one-third that of a prism with equal base and altitude (by subdividing into triangular pyramids).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop VI — Volume of a cylinder
rubrics_metrics.description: The volume of a cylinder equals the area of its base multiplied by its altitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by approximating the circular base with indefinitely many slender triangular prisms (elementary triangles) and summing; corollaries: (1) formula in terms of radius r and height h; (2) Guldinus-style result for solids of revolution (area × circumference of centroid path); (3) cone volume is one-third of cylinder with same base and altitude (limit or via pyramid/prism analogy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop VII — Surface area of a sphere equals cylindrical lateral surface
rubrics_metrics.description: The surface area of a sphere equals the convex (lateral) surface area of its circumscribed cylinder; consequently S = 4πr^2 and volume relations follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by comparing corresponding infinitesimal surface strips on sphere and cylinder (or via pyramidal decomposition using centre as vertex and surface patches as bases). Corollary: sphere volume is two-thirds of circumscribed cylinder; sphere surface equals area of rectangle by diameter and circumference of a great circle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appendix Exercises (volumes, surfaces, loci, proportionalities)
rubrics_metrics.description: A long list (numbered 1–30) of classical problems and results: surface area of cone, cylinder; proportionality and concurrency results for pyramids and tetrahedra; formulas for volumes of frusta and spherical segments; loci and visibility problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes specific notable items: convex surface of cone equals half rectangle (circumference × slant height); every plane section of a sphere is a circle; volumes and surface ratios between sphere and circumscribed solids (e.g., sphere:circumscribed cube as π:6); formulas for frustum volumes; concurrency properties of perpendiculars and bisecting planes in tetrahedra; many are stated as exercises for the reader to prove or apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Note A — Modern (projective) conception of the line at infinity
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduces the line at infinity and points at infinity: two lines with same point at infinity have same direction and are parallel; two with different points at infinity must meet in a finite point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a modern axiomatisation of parallelism: 'Any two lines in the same plane must meet at (1) infinity if same direction or (2) in some finite point if different directions.' References Poncelet and ties to axiomatic observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Note B — Independent proofs of triangle-angle-sum (Legendre & Hamilton)
rubrics_metrics.description: Presents two proofs of 'sum of angles of triangle equals two right angles' that are independent of the parallel-postulate theory: Legendre's iterative construction and Hamilton's (quaternion-inspired) rotational argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legendre's proof uses successive triangle constructions making one angle arbitrarily small; Hamilton's uses three rotations whose net rotation equals one full revolution, leading to angle-sum relations. Commentary notes limitations when applied to spherical geometry and gives historical attribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Note G — Quadrature of the circle and π discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion that π denotes the circumference-to-diameter ratio; area of a circle is πr^2; π is incommensurable (irrational) and must be approximated; gives notable rational approximations (22/7, 355/113) and mentions various elementary and advanced methods for computing π.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the problem of squaring the circle historically and points to approximation methods; supports the formulas used earlier for areas and volumes.
